items.abstract: <jats:p>General-purpose AI assistants are increasingly likely to be used in workplace psychosocial-riskrelated reflection and pre-assessment, yet most AI evaluations still focus on generic performance criteria. Rather than treating AI evaluation as a general performance question, this study introduces and applies an occupational health psychology and occupational health and safety (OHP/OHS)-grounded, domain-specific benchmarking logic for psychosocial risk management, with direct relevance to governance, responsible organizational use, and reporting practice. We benchmarked five leading assistant products across four standardized psychosocial-risk scenarios, three repetitions per scenario, and a fixed four-task sequence, yielding 60 archived conversations and 240 task-level outputs. Visible outputs were rated on Content Quality, Normative Alignment, Context Discipline, and Output Consistency under a blind second-rater design. Exact inter-rater agreement ranged from 0.454 to 0.679 across dimensions, while quadratic weighted kappa ranged from 0.131 to 0.394; within-1 agreement was 1.000 for all four dimensions. The pattern indicated directionally aligned but calibration-sensitive ratings, supporting the use of exact agreement and weighted kappa together rather than a single collapsed score. Claude showed the strongest blind descriptive profile across the three substantive dimensions, whereas the remaining products formed a lower and tighter cluster. The study shows that AI assistants can be compared in a structured and reviewer-auditable way for psychosocial risk management, while also showing why such comparison should remain dimension-specific, governance-relevant, and cautious in how it is reported.</jats:p>
title: Can AI Assistants Support Psychosocial Risk Management? An OHP/OHS-Grounded, Domain-Specific Benchmark

items.abstract: <jats:p>Background and Objective:Long-context large language model (LLM) assistants are increasingly used for biomedical research planning. A practical reliability risk is contextual carryover: obsolete entities or constraints from a previous task may contaminate a new experimental request after a deliberate topic switch. This study introduces a reproducible quality-assurance benchmark and analysis program for detecting contextual carryover in biomedical long-context AI assistants.Methods:The benchmark contains 1,600 matched synthetic biomedical task-switch prompts covering disease models, cell types, assays or omics modalities, candidate drugs, pathways, experimental goals, and safety or ethics constraints. The evaluation program combines sparse residual-stream diagnostics, risk-enriched stress testing, balanced non-enriched checks, same-backend counterfactual controls, direct-parent sensitivity analysis, auxiliary multi-model behavioral coverage, a deployment-oriented dry-run case study, and expert calibration. Two independent biomedical experts with more than ten years of domain experience annotated validation subsets, with adjudication by a senior experimental researcher with more than fifteen years of experience. Automated labels were produced by a fixed Qwen judge rubric and calibrated against expert labels.Results:Representation diagnostics showed that OpenBioLLM had stronger input-proximal old-entity anchoring but lower middle/late old-entity alignment and greater boundary separation than the general comparator. In same-backend counterfactual controls, OpenBioLLM showed a stronger original-A-specific obsolete-entity signal than Llama-3.1-70B (13.5% vs. 3.0%; Fisher&apos;s exact p = 0.000181). In a direct Llama-3 sensitivity subset (n = 382), aggregate semantic carryover was comparable between Llama-3 and OpenBioLLM (15.7% vs. 14.4%; paired difference -1.3 percentage points; bootstrap 95% CI -5.8 to 3.4; McNemar p = 0.653), but category-specific vulnerability differed. Balanced expert validation showed that the automated judge achieved 76.9% precision, 100.0% recall, 98.9% specificity, and 87.0% F1 against strict agreed human carryover labels. A 30-case deployment-oriented dry run showed no baseline carryover under the tested Llama-3.1 route (0/30) but detected one safety-context residue under a QA-intervention prompt (1/30), illustrating how the workflow can audit both assistant behavior and guardrail prompts before release.Conclusions:Contextual carryover is a measurable task-switching reliability risk in biomedical LLM assistants. The proposed benchmark is best interpreted as a reproducible quality-assurance program, regression test, and guardrail-prompt audit rather than a model leaderboard or a real-world prevalence estimator.</jats:p>
title: A Reproducible Quality-Assurance Benchmark for Detecting Contextual Carryover in Biomedical Long-Context AI Assistants

project-description.description:
Gaia AI Factory aims to establish a state-of-the-art AI Factory in Poland, creating a robust infrastructure for developing and deploying advanced artificial intelligence solutions. Coordinated by AGH University of Krakow’s ACC Cyfronet and supported by a national consortium of research and technology institutions, it responds to the growing demand for large-scale AI infrastructure in Europe. The initiative aligns with the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking’s mission to enhance Europe’s trustworthy AI capacity and with the Digital Europe Programme’s objective to ensure broad access to high-performance AI resources for research and innovation.

At its core lies a high-performance supercomputing system with around 1,000 GPU units divided into dedicated partitions for training and inference, enabling scalable processing for diverse AI applications — from research and prototyping to production. Gaia AI Factory offers not only infrastructure but a full innovation environment with pre-configured tools and end-to-end services for the AI lifecycle: data preparation, training, validation, deployment, and monitoring, accessible through a PLGrid-integrated portal.

Beyond technology, the Factory will foster collaboration among academia, industry, and the public sector through workshops, hackathons, and expert networks. It will also build human capacity via training programmes, online courses, and mentoring, enhancing national AI skills and workforce readiness. The Factory embeds principles of trustworthy and responsible AI, ensuring compliance with the AI Act, GDPR, and ethical governance.

Focusing on strategic domains — healthcare, space, and public administration — Gaia AI Factory supports innovation in diagnostics, satellite data analysis, and citizen services. Together with the PIAST AI Factory in Poznan and the LUMI AI Factory, Gaia will form a distributed, interoperable ecosystem for scalable, secure, and sustainable AI development. items.abstract: <jats:p>Website privacy policies are often lengthy and intricate. Privacy assistants assist in simplifying policies and making them more accessible and user-friendly. The emergence of generative AI (genAI) offers new opportunities to build privacy assistants that can answer users’ questions about privacy policies. However, genAI’s reliability is a concern due to its potential for producing inaccurate information. This study introduces GenAIPABench, a benchmark for evaluating Generative AI-based Privacy Assistants (GenAIPAs). GenAIPABench includes: 1) A set of curated questions about privacy policies along with annotated answers for various organizations and regulations; 2) Metrics to assess the accuracy, relevance, and consistency of responses; and 3) A tool for generating prompts to introduce privacy policies and paraphrased variants of the curated questions. We evaluated 3 leading genAI systems—ChatGPT-4, Bard, and Bing AI—using GenAIPABench to gauge their effectiveness as GenAIPAs. Our results demonstrate significant promise in genAI capabilities in the privacy domain while also highlighting challenges in managing complex queries, ensuring consistency, and verifying source accuracy.</jats:p>
title: GenAIPABench: A Benchmark for Generative AI-based Privacy Assistants

items.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>The Gaia benchmark stars are stars with very precise stellar parameters that cover a wide range in the HR diagram at various metallicities. They are meant to be good representative of typical FGK stars in the Milky Way. Currently, they are used by several spectroscopic surveys to validate and calibrate the methods that analyse the data. I review our recent activities done for these stars. Additionally, by applying our new method to find stellar twins on the Gaia‐ESO Survey, I discuss how good representatives of Milky Way stars the benchmark stars are and how they distribute in space.</jats:p>
title: Gaia benchmark stars and their twins in the Gaia‐ESO Survey
